summary: Argues that some firewalls wrongly reset TCP connections when they see SYN packets with flags set in the reserved field of the TCP header. This practice does not conform to TCP standards and misuses the meaning of a reset. It also considers the long-term effects. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: A reset tells someone you hang up the call. Some firewalls hang up simply because a message had an unfamiliar mark. This document says that is rude and breaks new features.

subtitle: Why a firewall should not answer a TCP SYN with a reset just because it uses a Reserved header flag, as with ECN.

tldr.problem: Some firewalls and load-balancers send a TCP reset in response to SYN packets that use flags from the Reserved field of the TCP header, which broke connections from ECN-capable hosts.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC argues from RFC 793 and RFC 1122 that this is not conformant: a reset is for segments not intended for the current connection. It also argues that overloading resets harms the evolution of TCP and the Internet.
tldr.outcome: Vendors are urged to fix the code and administrators to deploy the fixes. A firewall that wants to block a packet should drop it, not reset it.

today: RFC 3360 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 60) and, according to the metadata for this page, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. Its argument builds on RFC 793 and the ECN specification in RFC 3168.

sections.title: The Problem with Inappropriate Resets
sections.content:
TCP uses the RST (Reset) bit to abort a connection. Resets are appropriately sent in response to a connection request to a nonexistent connection, for example, and the receiver aborts the connection and tells the application.

The RFC reports that a number of firewalls and load-balancers send a reset in response to a SYN packet that uses flags from the Reserved field in the TCP header. Its main example is firewalls that reset SYN packets from ECN-capable hosts.

The document has two aims: to inform administrators of web servers and firewalls so they deploy bug-fixes, and to consider the longer-term effect of such middlebox behavior on how Internet protocols evolve.
sections.eli5: A reset is like hanging up the phone. It is fine when you dialed a wrong number. Some firewalls hang up when a call just has an unusual label on it.

sections.title: What the TCP Standards Say About Resets
sections.content:
RFC 793 defined the RST bit and explained that reset was devised to stop old duplicate connection initiations from causing confusion in the three-way handshake. It also says that a reset must be sent whenever a segment arrives which apparently is not intended for the current connection, and must not be sent if that is not clear.

RFC 1122 says nothing specific about resets in response to Reserved-field flags. So nothing in either RFC makes it acceptable to reset a SYN simply because it uses Reserved flags, and RFC 793 explicitly forbids doing so.

RFC 793 says the Reserved field is reserved for future use and must be zero. The RFC suggests a better phrasing would have been: zero when sent and ignored when received, unless future standards say otherwise. Even as written, it does not permit resets for a non-zero Reserved field.

The RFC also checks other places a reset is sanctioned and shows none of them applies. A mismatched precedence field is covered by RFC 2873, which says TCP must ignore precedence and must not reset on changes to it. An illegal option length (for example zero) may be reset according to RFC 1122, since the rest of the segment cannot be interpreted.

The robustness principle, "Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send", does not carry over clearly to firewalls. The related need for "adaptability to change" still matters.
sections.eli5: The rulebook says to hang up only when a call was meant for someone else. It never says to hang up because a call has a new sticker on it.

sections.title: The ECN Example
sections.content:
ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) lets routers set a bit in the IP header to signal congestion instead of dropping a packet. Both TCP end-nodes must support it and agree to use it for a given connection. The agreement uses two flags taken from the last two bits of the TCP Reserved field: bit 8 is Congestion Window Reduced (CWR) and bit 9 is ECN-Echo (ECE). The current definition comes from RFC 3168.

To negotiate, the sender transmits an ECN-setup SYN, a SYN with ECE and CWR set. A host willing to use ECN replies with an ECN-setup SYN-ACK, with ECE set and CWR not set. Otherwise it replies with neither flag set. An old TCP is expected to ignore the flags and send a plain SYN-ACK.

Some broken firewalls and load-balancers instead answer the ECN-setup SYN with a reset. After ECN-enabled hosts were deployed there were widespread complaints that they could not reach a number of websites. In March 2002, ECN-setup SYN packets were answered by a reset from 203 of the 12,364 web sites tested, and were dropped for 420 of them.
sections.eli5: Two friends agree to use a secret hand signal by putting a small mark on their first note. A few mail clerks tear up any note with an unfamiliar mark, so the friends cannot even say hello.

sections.title: The Work-Around and Its Cost
sections.content:
A host that gets a reset in reply to an ECN-setup SYN may resend the SYN with CWR and ECE cleared, which gives a connection without ECN. A host that gets no reply within the normal SYN retransmission timeout may likewise resend with the flags cleared, after possibly retransmitting one or more ECN-setup SYN packets first. RFC 3168 specifies this as a procedure that may be included in TCP implementations.

Some implementors chose not to deploy it. The work-around means the host does not respond properly to the first valid reset, can disable ECN where a SYN or SYN-ACK was simply lost, and in many cases adds a delay of six seconds or more when the broken equipment drops ECN-setup SYNs.

It also further erodes the meaning of a reset. The receiver cannot tell whether the reset was about the ECN flags or about a more fundamental problem, so it retries in a different form. The RFC warns this could become an extended spiral of changes to transport protocols.
sections.eli5: If the clerk tears up your note, you can write it again without the mark. That works, but now you never know why a note was torn up.

sections.title: Evolution of the Internet, and Advice for Hosts and Middleboxes
sections.content:
Equipment that rejects valid TCP packets that use Reserved flags could effectively prevent deployment of any new mechanism using those flags, however much IETF status the mechanism has. The RFC calls it a pity if TCP were frozen in its current state. This is one example of many small restrictions that together are a considerable obstacle to the development of the Internet architecture.

For transport protocols, the lesson is that they must protect themselves from the unknown actions of firewalls, normalizers and other middleboxes. For TCP, that means sending a non-ECN-setup SYN after a reset to an ECN-setup SYN. Protocols could use Reserved flags in the SYN before using them in data traffic, and may need to react to an ICMP "Communication Administratively Prohibited" message.

For middleboxes, the RFC argues that even a firewall that decides to drop packets using reserved bits should not send a reset. Resets are already used by some firewalls as a congestion control mechanism, and some popular TCP implementations immediately resend a SYN after a reset, up to four times. Adding a third meaning would give implementors an incentive to be even more persistent, leading to an escalation of measures and countermeasures. Dropping the packet does less damage, though it delays the sender. The RFC suggests firewalls willing to give explicit indications could send an ICMP Destination Unreachable message with code "Communication Administratively Prohibited", while admitting this is not ideal.

Some firewalls instead zero the Reserved flags. Zeroing them in the initial SYN is harmless, but zeroing them only in the SYN-ACK or in later packets could subvert end-to-end congestion control, as the appendix shows. The RFC concludes that if firewalls need to be able to block a new function, this is best addressed in the initial design phase by cooperation between the firewall community and protocol designers.
sections.eli5: If clerks keep tearing up anything new, nobody can ever invent a better note. It is kinder to quietly set a note aside, or better, to tell the sender why.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using Reserved flags risks revealing information about host configuration, but the RFC notes that port-scanning tools such as Nmap and Queso already identify configurations well without them. It cites one reported vulnerability: a packet filter meant to pass only packets of established connections could let through a packet not in an established connection if it had the ECE flag set.

The RFC also points out that misconceived security concerns helped cause the problem. An article described the Queso scanner as sending SYN packets with the last two Reserved bits set, which led middleboxes to block those bits. A lesson is that anyone can effectively attack a new TCP function by using it in a public port-scanning tool, causing middleboxes to block it.
sections.eli5: Some people blocked the secret hand signal because a troublemaker once used it. Now a good signal is blocked just because a bad person copied it.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that it is not conformant with current standards for a firewall, load-balancer or web server to respond with a reset to a TCP SYN simply because the packet uses flags in the TCP Reserved field. It urges vendors to make fixes available and ISPs and system administrators to deploy them.

It does not claim that dropping such packets violates a standard, but argues that doing so without a clear way to tell the end-nodes why could be a significant obstacle to the development of TCP. More work is needed to reconcile security with careful evolution of Internet protocols.
sections.eli5: Do not hang up just because of a new sticker. Fix the phone, and if you must block a call, do it quietly without making a mess of the rules.
